title: Lior and the Bridge
premise: In 1893, census taker Lior Ashcombe arrives at a fading river town to document its households and discovers that Edmund Thackeray, the reclusive apprentice clockmaker repairing the observatory's master clock, is a woman who has lived ten years as a man to inherit her dead father's workshop. As Lior's questions deepen into friendship and then love, the town's trustees move to seize the workshop on grounds of fraud, threatening both Edmund's identity and the clock she has promised to finish. When the census records become the instrument of her exposure, Edmund must choose between erasing herself from the ledger forever or signing her true name in public. She finishes the clock, testifies under her own name, loses the workshop but keeps her craft, and leaves with Lior for a city where no one knows which silences kept them safe.
about_author: Coral Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing Victorian census ledgers and apprenticeship papers in northern England. Her fiction excavates the small bureaucratic documents where hidden lives left their fingerprints.

chapters.title: The Ledger Opens
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Arriving by ferry, Lior begins the autumn census with methodical care, dreading the town's hostility toward outsiders. She hears rumors of the clockmaker who never attends church or market. The beat is quiet loneliness meeting professional resolve.

chapters.title: A Question of Households
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. At the Thackeray workshop, Edmund answers every question precisely until Lior asks whether anyone else sleeps in the house. The pause lasts too long. Edmund writes 'no' without looking up. The beat is the first crack in a decade of careful silence.

chapters.title: Escapement
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Working alone on the master clock's broken escapement, Edmund recalls her father's deathbed instruction: keep the name, lose the self. Ten years of binding her chest and her voice have made craft her only honest speech. The beat is grief hardened into discipline.

chapters.title: The Second Visit
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. A clerical error forces Lior back to the workshop. Edmund offers tea out of obligation; they argue about whether records tell truth. Lior notices Edmund's hands—calloused, ink-stained, unmistakably a worker's, and something else she can't name. The beat is reluctant fascination.

chapters.title: What the Clock Keeps
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Edmund shows Lior the master clock's interior, explaining how a mechanism can be honest even when its maker isn't. For the first time in years she speaks about her work without editing herself. The beat is dangerous intimacy disguised as instruction.

chapters.title: The Trustees' Meeting
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Invited to record town business, Lior witnesses trustee Aldous Crane propose auditing the Thackeray inheritance, citing 'irregularities' in the father's will. Lior realizes her own census sheets could serve as evidence. The beat is complicity arriving before choice.

chapters.title: Small Hours
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Unable to sleep, Edmund works through the night and finds Lior waiting outside at dawn, unable to sleep either. They walk the riverbank and talk about the towns they each escaped. The beat is two guarded people discovering matching locks.

chapters.title: The Apprentice's Hands
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Helping hold a gear assembly, Lior's fingers brush Edmund's and stay a moment too long. Later she rereads her census notes and notices what she recorded without understanding: 'lives alone; no wife.' The beat is desire entangled with suspicion.

chapters.title: Crane's Summons
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Crane visits the workshop with a copy of the apprenticeship indenture and asks pointedly why Edmund never married, never signed guild rolls under full name. Edmund lies fluently and shakes afterward. The beat is the past tightening like a mainspring.

chapters.title: What Lior Wrote
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Reviewing her completed sheets before submission, Lior finds Edmund's entry could expose her if subpoenaed. She faces a choice: alter an official record—a crime—or let bureaucracy do its work. The beat is conscience split down the middle.

chapters.title: The Name Beneath
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Searching her father's strongbox for the original will, Edmund finds instead a letter he never sent, addressed to 'my daughter,' proving he knew and loved her anyway. She weeps over gears for the first time since childhood. The beat is posthumous absolution.

chapters.title: Confession at the Observatory
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. In the clock tower at dusk, Lior tells Edmund she knows, and Edmund, exhausted by ten years of arithmetic survival, confirms it aloud. Neither names what it means yet. The beat is terror and relief arriving in the same breath.

chapters.title: Interlude of Ordinary Days
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Two weeks of stolen normalcy: shared suppers, Lior reading aloud while Edmund files brass, the clock ticking toward completion. Both know the audit looms but choose not to speak of it. The beat is borrowed happiness, deliberately unexamined.

chapters.title: The Subpoena
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Crane obtains a court order for the census sheets. Lior must surrender originals within the week. She drafts a falsified duplicate and hates herself for it, then burns the draft. The beat is the moment evasion stops being survivable.

chapters.title: Broken Escapement
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. A sabotaged part—she suspects Crane's man—destroys weeks of work days before the audit hearing. Edmund nearly abandons the clock entirely, then remembers her father's letter. The beat is despair transmuted into defiance.

chapters.title: Night Work
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. Lior abandons her official duties to help rebuild the escapement by lamplight, learning clockwork hands-on. They finish at dawn as the town wakes. The beat is love expressed purely as labor, side by side.

chapters.title: The Hearing
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Before the trustees, Crane presents the census sheet and demands Edmund account for the discrepancy. Cornered, Edmund could deny everything one more time. Instead she says: 'My name was Eleanor Thackeray.' The beat is the climax of self-erasure ending.

chapters.title: Verdict
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. The trustees void the inheritance; the workshop passes to Crane. But the guild examiner, moved by the finished master clock, certifies Eleanor as a journeyman clockmaker—the first under any name. The beat is loss and legitimacy in the same gavel-fall.

chapters.title: Emptying the Workshop
chapters.summary: Eleanor's POV. Packing tools, Eleanor finds her father's letter again and adds her own beside it—for whoever comes next. Lior arrives with train tickets and no speech prepared. The beat is mourning a place while refusing to mourn oneself.

chapters.title: The Last Wind
chapters.summary: Eleanor's POV. Eleanor starts the master clock one final time and leaves it running for the town that rejected its maker. From the ferry she watches the observatory dial catch morning light. The beat is bittersweet release; the work outlives the welcome.

chapters.title: A New Ledger
chapters.summary: Lior's POV. In the city, Lior resigns from the census office and takes work with a reform society documenting women workers' lives—this time with consent. Eleanor signs her first guild contract: E. Thackeray, journeyman. The beat is turning instruments of exposure into instruments of witness.

chapters.title: What Keeps Time
chapters.summary: Shared final chapter, alternating voices. A year later, in their small flat above a repair shop, Eleanor builds clocks under her own name while Lior writes. On the mantel sits the old workshop key. The beat is quiet resolution: identity, love, and craft all keeping time together.
